title: Store the Record
content:
What problem does this solve?
A static log is not enough. If the program must rewrite every sentence as the overdue count changes, it is not modeling the expedition. Variables let you name information, change it, and reuse it later.

Basic syntax
  name = expression

What actually happens
The right-hand side is evaluated first. Then Python attaches that resulting value to the name on the left. A variable is a label pointing at a value, not a fixed box that permanently owns one type.

A string is text in quotes, such as "OVERDUE". An integer is a whole number without quotes, such as 17. An expression is anything Python can evaluate, including a name, a number, or days_overdue + 1. Reassignment makes the same name point at a new value.

When this is useful
Use named values whenever a fact may change — days overdue, party size, or status — so print() can reuse the current values without rewriting the whole program. You already know print() from the last lesson; now print named values instead of only literals.
concepts: Assignment evaluates the right side, then binds the name on the left
Strings are quoted text; integers are whole numbers without quotes
Variable names should describe meaning (days_overdue, not x)
Reassigning a name makes it point at a new value
Expressions can combine named values with arithmetic

examples.title: Changing record
examples.code:
expedition = 17
days_overdue = 2
print(expedition)
print(days_overdue)
days_overdue = days_overdue + 1
print(days_overdue)
examples.explanation: days_overdue starts at 2. After reassignment with days_overdue + 1, the same name refers to 3.

common_mistakes: Writing status == "OVERDUE" when you meant to assign ( == compares; = assigns )
Using a variable before assigning it — that raises NameError
Forgetting quotes around literal text: OVERDUE without quotes looks like a variable name
Hardcoding a calculated result instead of building it from the named values

exercises.title: Predict the changing record
exercises.prompt: What does this program print? Type each line of output.
hints: Trace the value of days_overdue from top to bottom.
The second assignment uses the current value of days_overdue on the right-hand side.
First print shows 2; after adding 1, the second print shows 3.
exercises.failure_message: Re-read the reassignment line carefully — the name on the right still holds the old value when that expression is evaluated.

exercises.title: Complete the calculation
exercises.prompt: Replace the placeholder so evidence_count is the sum of tracks_found and damaged_items. Build the value from both variable names — do not hardcode the result.
exercises.starter_code:
tracks_found = 2
damaged_items = 3
evidence_count = 0  # TODO: replace 0 with an expression using both variables
print(evidence_count)
hints: evidence_count should be calculated from the two named values above it.
Use + to combine the integers those names refer to.
Replace None with an expression that mentions tracks_found and damaged_items.

tests.name: evidence_count
tests.message: Build evidence_count from tracks_found and damaged_items, not a hardcoded number.

exercises.title: Repair the status
exercises.prompt: This program should store the word OVERDUE as literal text in status, then print it. Fix the assignment.
hints: Without quotes, Python treats OVERDUE as a variable name.
Literal text must be a string.

exercises.title: Build an expedition record
exercises.prompt:
Create these variables:
  expedition -> the integer 17
  registered -> the integer 4
  days_overdue -> the integer 3
  status -> the string "OVERDUE"

Then print each value on its own line in that order, using the variable names — do not copy-paste the values into print().
exercises.starter_code: # Create the expedition record, then print each value
hints: Strings need quotes; integers do not.
Assign all four names first, then call print four times with those names.
Print expedition, registered, days_overdue, and status — the variables themselves, not quoted copies of the numbers.

tests.message: Print the variable names themselves, not hardcoded literal values.

exercises.success_message: Record stored. The overdue counter and party count are now named values your program can reuse.
